final_proof:
Let \(\zeta=e^{2\pi i/n}\). Because \(e^{2\pi i(k+n)/n}=e^{2\pi i k/n}\), the indexing in the definition of \(U_n\) may be replaced by the complete residue system \(k=0,1,\ldots,n-1\). Thus put \(v_k=\zeta^k=e^{2\pi i k/n}\) for \(0\le k<n\). These points are pairwise distinct: if \(v_j=v_k\), then \(e^{2\pi i(j-k)/n}=1\), so \((j-k)/n\) is an integer. Since \(|j-k|<n\), this forces \(j=k\). Hence the \(v_k\) are precisely the \(n\) elements of \(U_n\).

Every \(v_k\) has modulus one, so all these points lie on the unit circle centered at the origin. Their arguments in counterclockwise order are
\[
0,\frac{2\pi}{n},\frac{4\pi}{n},\ldots,\frac{2(n-1)\pi}{n}.
\]
Consequently, every pair of successive points, including \(v_{n-1}\) and \(v_0\), subtends the same central angle \(2\pi/n\). Join successive points in this cyclic order and denote the resulting polygon by \(P\). Since \(n\ge3\), the points are distinct, and chords joining consecutive points in their order on a circle form a convex \(n\)-gon.

Consider rotation about the origin through angle \(2\pi/n\), which in complex notation is the map \(w\mapsto\zeta w\). It sends \(v_k\) to \(v_{k+1}\), with indices taken modulo \(n\), and therefore sends each side of \(P\) to the next side and each interior vertex angle to the next interior vertex angle. Since rotations preserve lengths and angles, all sides of \(P\) have the same length and all its interior angles are equal. Thus \(P\) is a regular \(n\)-sided polygon. Explicitly, its common side length is
\[
|v_{k+1}-v_k|=|\zeta-1|=2\sin\!\left(\frac{\pi}{n}\right).
\]

The unit circle contains every vertex of \(P\), so it is the circle circumscribed about \(P\), and its center is the complex number \(0\), corresponding to \((0,0)\). Moreover, \(v_0=e^0=1\), corresponding to \((1,0)\), so one of the vertices has the required location.

Finally, the hypothesis concerning \(z\) is consistent with, and in fact characterizes, this vertex set. If \(z^n=1\), then \(|z|^n=1\), whence \(|z|=1\). Write \(z=e^{i\theta}\). Then \(e^{in\theta}=1\), so \(n\theta=2\pi m\) for some \(m\in\mathbb Z\). Hence \(z=e^{2\pi i m/n}=v_k\), where \(k\in\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\) is the residue of \(m\) modulo \(n\). Thus every \(n\)th root of unity is one of the vertices just described.
